I am 72 years old, and I have farmed these fields in Quzhou County since I was fifteen. My father taught me, and his father taught him. The land here on the North China Plain is good black soil, but it is tired now, and water is not as easy to come by as it once was. I only went to primary school, but I know this land better than any book-learned expert. I have six mu of land, and I do not try to be clever with it. Every year I plant winter wheat after the autumn harvest, and every June after the wheat comes off, I put in summer maize. That is the rotation that works here, and I will not change it now.

My wheat went into the ground last October, as it always does. I used an improved wheat seed — not the old traditional grains, which do not yield enough to feed a family anymore, but a variety I have used for years that stands up to the wind and the cold. Right now it is April, and the wheat is greening up. I will irrigate it four times before harvest: the overwinter irrigation was already done, and now I will water at jointing, heading, and grain filling. I spread about twenty-two jin of nitrogen fertilizer per mu in split applications, plus some phosphate and potash. I will spray three times for weeds and insects because if you do not stay on top of them, they will take everything. Before I planted the wheat, I ploughed the field deep to break up the hardpan. I expect about nine hundred jin per mu — around four hundred and fifty kilos — which is a decent harvest if the weather holds.

When the wheat comes off in early June, I will immediately plant hybrid maize. Hybrid corn grows fast and gives good yields, though the seed costs more. I will use the rotary tiller because at my age I cannot handle the plough like I used to, and the rotary machine is faster. The maize needs less fuss than wheat — two good irrigations, a bit less fertilizer, and two pesticide sprays. If the summer rains cooperate, I should get about eleven hundred jin per mu, maybe five hundred and fifty kilos. I thought about renting out my land to a younger farmer or a company, but the rent they offer is not enough to live on, and farming is what I know. This wheat and maize will feed my family and give me grain to sell. I do not have time or strength for vegetables or strange new crops. Wheat and maize are what the market here wants, and they are what I will grow.
